items.question: How do you assess whether your approach to building Nano Banana as a generalist agent paid off?
items.object: Nano Banana’s generalist approach and public reception
items.answer: What we tried to do this time around was we wanted to approach the problem kind of bottom up and build a really generalist agent. We released this to LM Marina under the code name Nano Banana. The ELO scores ended up being really high, and we had a big improvement over other models. I think we had a couple million votes on Elmar Marina, which at the time was equal to all of the text model votes up to that point. So there was much more interest than we anticipated. But I think when we saw that, it was really encouraging that, oh, this model is actually really useful for people.

items.question: How do you understand the growing role of large AI labs in developing tools for creative work?
items.object: The growing role of foundation models and AI labs in creative tools
items.answer: I think for a long time in the field we would solve problems for creative applications, creative tools, and for content creation on a case-by-case basis. During this time, some of the best groups of people working on these problems were at the media companies. I think what we've seen happen with AI is there's been more of an emphasis on using the world knowledge and all the other powerful tools that come out of large language models. It turns out that those are actually very useful for creative tasks. So I think we see the big foundation model and these big AI labs taking more of a role in this space simply because the tools exist in these large language models that can really help with creative tasks.

items.question: Why do you think creative work has become one of the first areas where AI models are useful?
items.object: Creative work as an early application of AI
items.answer: I also think the creative tasks are a little bit counterintuitive. People often thought that the creative realm was going to be the last one that gets touched by AI. But actually, because there's many possible answers you can get from an AI model that are useful for different creative tasks, for ideation or for iteration, it turns out that this is one of the first places that the models are useful. So a lot of things start in the creative realm and I think maybe move later into other factuality spaces. I think we're seeing this as well for images too.

items.answer: You get a lot of emergent behavior once the model has all the world knowledge in it, and it makes doing things that used to be really hard much easier.

items.question: What do you see as the important advances in Nano Banana, officially Gemini 2.5 Flash Image?
items.object: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image)
items.answer: Nano Banana, whose official name is Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, is our latest and best image model. It can do generation and editing, importantly, which means you can have a conversation with an agent where you iterate on editing an image to get it to the point that you want. And this is another model in a line of image models that we've released at Google. We have the Imagen line, and we released Gemini Flash Image 2.0. So this is the next version of that. I think we really were able to make a lot of improvement for this model, and we've seen the usage take off because of that.

items.question: What do you see as the main advances in Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, also known as Nano Banana, compared with Imagen?
items.object: Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (Nano Banana) compared with Imagen
items.answer: The thing that we're really proud of in the Gemini 2.5 Flash Image model is that we've integrated it into Gemini, which means we can take advantage of all the world knowledge I was talking about earlier. For Imagen, you can generate very good images, but you have to be very explicit about what you want to generate. With Nano Banana, it's possible to have prompts that are much more seeking input or information from the AI model itself. So we see people asking highly abstract prompts, and the model is able to do a much better job of deciding what it is the user is trying to ask and then coming up with a reasonable response and image to satisfy this request. I think that's the main thing that we're seeing. We have a lot more world knowledge. We can have a lot better understanding of what users are trying to do. We can operate more autonomously as a result. The second thing is that we can also use it for editing images, or any kind of conversational editing, which has opened a lot of doors as well.

items.question: How do you understand Gemini 2.5 Flash Image as an integrated Gemini model when users select it separately?
items.object: Gemini 2.5 Flash Image’s integration into Gemini
items.answer: When I say integrated, I guess I mean that, yes, you select the Gemini 2.5 Flash Image model in a dropdown, but that model you can then ask text questions to, you can ask coding questions, you can ask image generation questions. So it's a fully fledged language model with all the world knowledge of Gemini. It is a separate checkpoint that has the image capabilities in it, but it is a sort of unified Gemini experience. This model is new, and we're seeing where it can be successful and where it can't be successful. items.question: Why do you think building Nano Banana as a general-purpose image editing and generation model helped its adoption?
items.object: Nano Banana’s general-purpose image editing and generation design
items.answer: We've had editing capabilities in our image models before. What we tried to do this time around was approach the problem kind of bottom up and build a really generalist agent, and I think that was key for its success in adoption. Instead of being trained to do one or two tasks really well, this model can perform a very wide variety of edits, and some of the edits that we've seen take off and be used by the public are things that we never really anticipated. We're kind of surprised ourselves in seeing the creative uses that people come up with for the model. So I view this as an attempt to build a general-purpose image editing and generation model.

items.question: What did you find most telling about Nano Banana’s reception on LM Arena?
items.object: Nano Banana’s reception on LM Arena as evidence of usefulness
items.answer: We were proud of what we had, and we released this to LM Arena under the code name Nano Banana. This was supposed to be our anonymous code name just for the LM Arena release, and we saw it take off much steeper than we expected. The ELO scores ended up being really high, and we had a big improvement over other models. That was great. But the real indication that this model was going to be somewhat successful is that we had so many users coming to LM Arena to use Nano Banana. Even if they were only getting it some random percentage of the time, it still ended up being a huge driver in traffic, and we had to emergency increase our QPS support for LM Arena. I think we had a couple million votes on LM Arena, which at the time was equal to all of the text model votes up to that point. There was much more interest than we anticipated. items.question: How do you understand the distinction between generation and image editing in a multimodal model like Gemini?
items.object: Generation and image editing in Gemini
items.answer: I think it's kind of a misnomer to say that it's a focus on editing. Gemini is a multimodal model, and it can handle multimodal inputs and multimodal outputs. This is the most general form of interaction. The differentiation between generation and editing is just: what are the modalities of input the model can take? If you can only take text as input, then you're doing generation. But if you can take images as input as well, you're doing editing. So they're not really separate modalities, at least in my head. It's just the uses that people have for them. Once your model is general in the types of inputs that it can take, it could do either of those things.

items.question: Why do you consider faithfulness to the input image so important for high-fidelity image editing?
items.object: Faithfulness to input images in high-fidelity image editing
items.answer: That's an intentional choice to support this type of high-fidelity edit. I think that's a really important part, especially if you consider that most people are interested in, for example, putting themselves into another situation or people they know. As humans, we're very sensitive to the details in people's faces that define identity. So if you get it wrong just a little bit, it's instantly noticeable: that's not me, that's not my kids. So we did put a lot of effort into making sure that the model had good faithfulness to the input, the context.

items.question: How do you understand the apparent leap in image-editing capability that comes from preserving consistency with an input image?
items.object: The apparent leap in image-editing model capabilities
items.answer: I would say there's not one thing that we did as to why this works. It's really a culmination of many years of experience working in the space and figuring out over time all the different parts of the recipe and how to tweak it to make it better and better. The improvement behind the scenes is a much smoother, linear ramp, and then on the outside, you cross a point where the model becomes more useful. So it looks like these big jumps. But it feels like this is something we've been working on for a long time to get to this point.

items.question: How do you see the respective roles of model capabilities and training data in achieving high-fidelity, consistent image edits?
items.object: The interplay between model capabilities and training data in high-fidelity image editing
items.answer: Of course I won't be able to give you a fully satisfactory answer, unfortunately. But I will say that it's not either-or. Both of the things have to be right to work. You need a model that can generate this much detail and preserve detail from the context, and you need data to be able to train the model to do that. So it's really the interplay between the two. If you just go for one of them, you won't get there. It's really everything. I hear that the model being able to generate sufficient detail is a very broad capability, and then on top of that, you want to layer the ability to do a good job at specific things, and that is primarily data.

items.question: Why do you find educational uses of models that combine world knowledge and image generation exciting?
items.object: Educational uses of models that combine world knowledge and image generation
items.answer: I saw some posts on X where people had taken the model and written a geometry problem for it to solve. So you imagine a triangle and one of the sides is labeled X, and then you can ask the model to solve for X, and it will do it in the image space, which is really cool. This is a direction I think is really exciting with these general multi-purpose models with world knowledge. If you think about the way that we humans learn, or a textbook, there's always lots of images. I think we need to move past this idea that language models communicate via text, because many things are just explained better in images or videos. Seeing signs of life of useful information-seeking or educational use cases just emerge from this joint world-knowledge image-generation model is really cool.

items.answer: I think there's definitely quite a large set of creative professionals who could benefit from using these techniques. items.question: How do you see the uses of image generation models evolving beyond creative work?
items.object: The future applications of image generation models
items.answer: I think we're at a stage like when GPT-1 and 2 came out, people were like, 'Oh, this is a cool model. I can use it to write haikus about funny topics,' and people are doing a lot of these creative use cases because it's more forgiving and you can riff on things and take them. I think we're there with image generation as well. Historically, and up until now, probably the majority of use cases have been for creative professionals or casual creative users. But I think we're moving into a point where, if you look at what people are using language models for now, the use case is much broader. People are using it for information-seeking queries and talking to agents about things, working through problems. I think all these use cases have visual components to the communication process, and we could end up seeing these models play a role in those areas too. In my opinion, that's the trajectory we're going on and what we'll see from the next generation of image models as we improve the factuality and reliability of the images generated.

items.question: How do you see node-based image-generation workflows evolving as models become able to handle more tasks in one shot?
items.object: Node-based image-generation interfaces and elaborate creative workflows
items.answer: I love node-based interfaces, to be honest. UI is amazing. I absolutely don't see those going away. As we push the model to be more useful and to one-shot more use cases, it'll be more accessible for people using it. But there's always going to be creative people who are really pushing the boundaries and figuring out, 'If I combine this with this and this really complicated workflow, then they can do amazing new things.' I never underestimate the ability for humans to get tired of the thing that they get used to. There's always going to be this need for creative people to push the boundary, do things that are not just easy to do with models, squeeze more juice out of them, and make more impressive stuff. So I don't think that's going away. What I do think we're getting to is the point where more people can use the models to make a birthday card really easily. But on the high end, the space is even more opened up, because if you give people more tools, they can do more creative, amazing things.

items.object: Nano Banana’s integration into creative tools and developer-built interfaces

items.question: How do you think about the tradeoff between giving users granular control over open-source AI models and offering hosted models through simple APIs?
items.object: User control in open-source and hosted AI models
items.answer: There's always this kind of push and pull between how many levers you want to expose. When you have open-source models, people will hack in everything and you can have full control. With the hosted models, we try to give controls so the users can really do a broad variety of things. I would like to see more ability for hackers to do things that would be cool on the models. I think the ecosystem is large enough for both the open-source models that are fully hackable and people can run local inference on, as well as the hosted models that are run by APIs. I think we'll see both of those. Figuring out how to merge the really complicated node-based interface with thousands of edges and a pretty simple API interface for the majority of people is an interesting challenge, and it's one we're still working on.

items.question: How do you see the role of fine-tuning versus in-context examples for Nano Banana?
items.object: Fine-tuning versus in-context examples for Nano Banana
items.answer: I think it's an interesting question. I'll make the analogy again to language models, where I think there was a lot more fine-tuning, and then people realized they could do a lot of stuff with putting their fine-tuning data in context and just trying to prompt in context. Bottom line is, I think professional use cases will probably benefit from fine-tuning, and we're hopeful that the majority of use cases can benefit from just having examples in context. But we don't offer a fine-tuning service for the model right now.

items.question: How do you see the long-term usefulness of fine-tuning image and vision-language models?
items.object: Fine-tuning image and vision-language models
items.answer: I think fine-tuning will always be a useful capability on top of models. If you're trying to generate scenes from a specific show with specific characters, you could fine-tune these models on your data and have it do a better job generating these characters. I think we do see quite a few use cases like that. Also, for brands, to be able to fine-tune models on their brand looks makes a lot of sense. I don't think fine-tuning is going away, but maybe in the long run we need it less and less. I think it'll still be useful, and these models can be fine-tuned just like any language models or image models out there.

items.question: How do you assess the room for improvement in the quality of image-generation models?
items.object: Image-generation model quality
items.answer: I don't think we're anywhere near the ceiling for quality. Improving the quality of these models will make them more useful. We get to the point now where, if you know what to do, you can cherry-pick a really good image out of most of the top models, and it'll be exactly what you want. But if you're just exploring the models, as soon as you leave this comfortable space of things that work really well, you can fall into, 'Oh yeah, this doesn't work,' or 'This doesn't look right,' or 'It's not what I was trying to create.' We still have a number of years ahead of us for making these models better, and every time they're made better, they'll become more useful. That's ignoring the whole world-knowledge aspect, which I think is coming with all the information-seeking use cases.

items.question: How do you see scaling as a way to improve image generation models?
items.object: Scaling image generation models
items.answer: One thing is, of course, scale. We're seeing what happens at scale. I think the image community has been behind the language models for scaling up their models and figuring out how to do it. A lot of people have tried, but it's very hard to successfully scale up an image model to be the same size as our language models and still see gains. So there are questions like: how do we scale the models, and if we do scale them, what's the impact? That's one thing that's kind of unknown at this time, but interesting.

items.question: Why do you see evaluating image generation models as significantly harder than evaluating text models?
items.object: Evaluating image and media generation models
items.answer: Maybe this is a bit in the weeds, but evaluation of the models is significantly harder than text models. A lot of times we're trying to—there's no clear right and wrong answers. A lot of what the model does, how do you know it's getting better? A lot of it is personal preference, and there's a wide variety of personal preference that different people have. Something that's getting better for one person may be getting worse for another person. So it makes it interesting trying to figure out how to hill-climb different aspects of your model and still measure whether it's getting better or not. This is something people who work on images and media generation really struggle with, but I'm excited to see what people come up with as proxies or ways that people can predict quality.

items.answer: From the beginning there's always been aesthetic models that people have used, and these are typically trained with pairwise human preference scores. items.question: How do you think about optimizing image generation models for large-scale human preferences?
items.object: Optimizing image generation models for large-scale human preferences
items.answer: It's very hard to say that's the best model. If you optimize for very large-scale preference, you end up with maybe something that's generic and doesn't have character or generate interesting images. If you look at Midjourney, for example, they've spent a lot of effort on having stylistic control and being able to generate images personalized to users' stylistic preferences. This is very useful for their users in generating these really nice images. I think there are a lot of different ways people can do it. I don't think we actually know what the best way is.

items.question: How do you see Nano Banana's strengths and limitations as an image editing model?
items.object: Nano Banana's strengths and the tradeoff between instruction following and creative exploration
items.answer: I think the things it's best at are preserving the content and people's identity in images that you edit. I think this is one of the reasons why it took off when we released the first version. I don't think it's an artistic model like a Midjourney model. If you put a random prompt in, you don't expect to get back something that looks amazing. We try to make it really expressible and put a lot of effort into making sure that it's following the user instructions as closely as possible. Sometimes for creative tasks those two things are a little contradictory, because you might want to take the user away from the thing they're asking because it's more interesting or cool to look at. Because we've pushed for a really controllable model and a high amount of instruction following, it's maybe less suitable for creative exploration tasks.

items.object: Prompting accessibility and expert control in Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (Nano Banana)
items.answer: We try to make it so you can give very simple input and get a reasonable output. items.answer: I'm not going to call out any specific papers. I've seen a lot of very good papers. This is a space where the forefront is being pushed by the big labs that are usually keeping secrets pretty close to themselves. I like spaces when the academic community is leading and every paper is amazing and going to change the field. I think we'll get back to that point again at some point. items.question: How do you see the accessibility of vision-language model research for enthusiasts working outside big labs?
items.object: Small-scale vision-language model research outside big labs
items.answer: For enthusiasts in the area, it's completely possible to have a home setup and do interesting work and interesting research. The required boilerplate to get systems like these up and training is pretty well supported with today's tools. The things that you can't do at a smaller scale are training models that are across all axes. But I think it's definitely possible to take some narrow data slice and do experiments and make improvements in a small, constrained way, and those are things that'll probably set you up for knowing how the larger systems work. It's definitely not inaccessible just because we have these big, well-resourced groups pushing the frontier of quality. I don't think that means it's inaccessible technology for people to pick up. I think it's quite accessible. You can get a baseline running, totally doable by one excited person in their room over a couple months.

items.answer: I mentioned earlier the evaluation problem, and well-thought-out evaluations and testing domains are still really interesting. I saw this great paper on vision-language models about how they're fooled by—it's called the illusion illusion—and it's about how if you give the model something that's not actually an illusion but is close to an illusion, it'll be fooled into thinking it's an illusion.

items.question: How do you understand a vision model’s response to a modified checkerboard-and-shadow optical illusion?
items.object: Vision models’ responses to a modified checkerboard-and-shadow optical illusion
items.answer: An example I would give is an optical illusion. There's the classic one where you have the checkerboard and the shadow of a cylinder, and these two squares are the same color, right? We've all seen that image a lot of times, even though our brains interpret them as different colors because one is in the shadow. It turns out if you give it to a vision model and you make them very different colors, it'll still say, 'Oh, these are the same color because it's seen the illusion before.'

items.answer: In the generation space people have been playing with trying to get full wine glasses for a while, and it's the same concept, right? We've seen so many wine glasses that are not quite full that it's very difficult to get a full wine glass. This is something that's very easy to do and really can be done distributed, and I do see a lot of interesting work coming out on evaluating where these models fail and where they don't. items.question: How do you see the potential of verifiable domains for improving image generation?

items.answer: You could imagine if you generate multiple camera views of a scene, you could do some 3D reconstruction and see if it actually makes sense. Then these maybe can inform reward signals. I think this is an interesting space. The problem I see is coming up with a way to get a wide enough range of these verifiable domains that you can then generalize to being good at everything else. Here we're talking mostly about accuracy, which is definitely a big thing we want to improve, but we also have to consider aesthetics, which is much harder to measure. Is the lighting nice on this image? It's much more difficult to tell whether we've succeeded in that space. I think probably if you target a few verifiable domains and figure out how to maximize quality in these spaces, it will be beneficial in other areas, but I haven't seen much of this yet.

items.object: The tension between accuracy and aesthetics in image generation
items.answer: I think as a community we're just starting to get to this point, because we've been working really hard on just making the images not be full of artifacts. I feel like these kinds of six fingers and—

items.question: How do you see the relationship between aesthetics and accuracy changing as image generation models improve?
items.object: The relationship between visual aesthetics and accuracy in image generation models
items.answer: We just got to five fingers, and until we got to five fingers, all the improvements are benefiting both of these axes because you still need an image that's structurally sound in order to be either correct or aesthetic, or believable as an image. I don't think we've yet really struggled with this, but I do think we're starting to get to the point where different teams can take different roads, where they optimize for one or the other. In some sense it's a data distribution problem: if you're able to narrow your data distribution into just the good-looking images, it can actually be easier to generate those because it's a narrower distribution, so it's easier to model. A lot of what we did at the beginning of these image models was figure out how to restrict the generation to a very small subset of things that looked reasonable. In the process, that was also the way to generate the best images. Now as we get better at modeling and can model this wider distribution of things that maybe look good and things that don't look good but have interesting information in them, it opens up more avenues for us to do both at the same time in the same model. We're broadening the distribution of things we can generate well enough that it's not just instantly thrown out. Is it supposed to generate things that look good? Is it supposed to generate things that are accurate and believable? What's the purpose?

items.question: How do you understand the idea that an image generation model can produce aesthetically pleasing images while covering only a narrow range of aesthetics?
items.object: Aesthetic diversity in image generation models
items.answer: I think it's a bit of a precision-recall thing, because if you have a model that can generate only aesthetic things, it doesn't mean that you're generating all the aesthetic things. You haven't covered everything that's aesthetic, but you've restricted yourself to only generating things that look good. That's the kind of narrow view that was a starting place and was easier to generate. Now that we can have models that generate broader distributions, we probably can get a better recall of things that different people would find aesthetically pleasing. Maybe someone really likes crayon scribbles. This is something that we can do now that we have a broader distribution. I'm not saying that we covered everything that everybody has ever liked, but at the beginning we focused on things people did like.

items.question: Why do you think the recognizable AI look has become a problem for image generation models?
items.object: The recognizable AI look of generated images
items.answer: What's interesting is that this AI look came out of that first round of trying to narrow the distribution to things that we can generate well and still look good. People got saturated by it. Now it's a problem if your model generates only these things in this AI look. The tastes are changing as well, because when that first came out, everyone was so amazed that you could generate those things that it was still really cool and fun to play in that AI-looking space. Now people expect more, so we need to be able to generate more broad images.

items.question: How do you think about the value and risks of using AI-generated images as training data?
items.object: AI-generated images as training data
items.answer: I think it's definitely a problem. You don't want to add a bunch of bad AI-generated images into your training data, because you'll learn to generate bad AI-generated images. I think the same thing exists in the tech space as well. This concept of AI slop is interesting too, because there's also good images, and it's a little less clear: do you actually want to train on good images or not? There's been some distillation process by which people have said, 'Oh, that's a really good image,' and we know that if you can distill synthetic data to the point where it's high quality, it can actually be beneficial to train on. So it's not that all AI-generated images are necessarily detrimental, but the bad ones are. There are a couple interesting problems: how do we handle the fact that there's more AI-generated images and AI-generated text out there that we don't necessarily want to train on, because we might learn factual inaccuracies or unrealistic lighting, with the fact that some of this data is highly curated and people think it's really good and the quality might be much higher? How do we tell the difference between those two? These are all interesting problems.

items.question: How do you see the limits of training an image generator on good images from a narrow domain?
items.object: Training on good images from a narrow domain
items.answer: I think if you have only produced good images in a narrow band or domain, training on just that band or domain doesn't necessarily help you get to a broader ability to generate more diverse, aesthetically pleasing images.
quotes: if you have only produced good images in a narrow band or domain, training on just that band or domain doesn't necessarily help you get to a broader ability to generate more diverse, aesthetically pleasing images.

rubrics.text: The response states that training an image generator exclusively on good images from a narrow domain does not necessarily generalize to good image generation beyond that domain.

items.question: How do you think about the limits of training AI models on their own synthetic data?
items.object: Training AI models on synthetic data and the balance between human and synthetic supervision
items.answer: I think that's something that has been a topic of discussion in AI for a while: how much can you eat your own tail? Is it possible to train models on fully synthetic data and use self-supervision? A lot of people have been looking at different parts of this, and I think how much human supervision versus synthetic supervision is needed. I don't think we know the answers to these questions, and everything that exists in the text space has an analogy in images.

items.question: How do you view the tradeoff between scaling image models and carefully curating their training data?
items.object: Model scaling versus data curation for training image models
items.answer: There's always discussions. Like I said earlier, we're just scratching the surface, and it's possible that someone could come up with a much more efficient recipe that does way better and is more compute efficient. I think there's still a lot of gains that are going to be made by the community in this area. I wouldn't predict which direction we're going: is it all going to be finding the exact right data points to train a small model on, or scaling everything up ten times bigger and hoping it all works out? I'm not going to predict which one is the winner.

items.question: How do you think image-generation models will make their next major improvements?
items.object: The potential for further progress in image-generation models
items.answer: I don't know how far we'd get by scaling naively. If I look at the text side, I feel like we saw a huge boost in accuracy when all the main labs started doing thinking, test-time scaling, and that ended up being really important. These ideas can still land in images. Test-time scaling images is something we haven't really figured out quite yet, and probably all the labs are trying different ways to solve this problem. I would say that it's not that the recipes are well known. I hope we get to the point where everyone starts publishing again and we can see what we've all been doing, because maybe we'll be able to put our heads together and figure out what actually mattered. Barring that, discoveries will happen independently, but people will figure these types of things out. It's a lot easier to do something when you've seen it be done. When other labs make progress and you're like, 'Oh, this is possible,' then you know what to try because you can see that something could work. There is this lifting up of the models, just the fact that we have all these different labs working on them. I do expect large improvements coming. We also saw with G3 that interactivity is on the horizon, and these world models that you can walk around and interact with components of are all really early and just launching and very exciting. The space is really open with possibility.
